newsitem.title: USA: Hamas leader withdraws U.S. extradition appeal.
newsitem.headline: Hamas leader withdraws U.S. extradition appeal.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent
The head of the political arm of the militant Palestinian group Hamas has withdrawn his appeal of a ruling that would allow his extradition to Israel, his lawyers said on Wednesday.

The decision by Mousa Mohammed Abu Marzook to drop the challenge means he can be sent back to Israel within about 60 days. His lawyers told a news conference he decided to abandon the appeal despite their feeling that they had a strong case.

They said their client had lost faith in the U.S. justice system after being imprisoned for 18 months without being charged with a crime. "We are witnessing an evolution of despair," New York lawyer Michael Kennedy said.

Israel announced in 1995 that it had formally asked the United States to hand over Abu Marzook, who was arrested in July of that year at a New York airport as he flew to the United States, where he had lived for at least 15 years.

Israel alleged that he was responsible, as head of the political arm of the Islamic resistance movement Hamas, for attacks that killed scores of Israelis. It did not contend that he had personally carried out violent acts.

Abu Marzook argued he had been involved only in political matters, which are not extraditable offences. But a U.S. district judge ordered his extradition last May, saying he was involved in an "agreement to accomplish an unlawful act."

The judge refused to allow a hearing on Abu Marzook's argument that the offences charged by Israel were not covered by the treaty with the United States because of the political offence exception. Abu Marzook's lawyers said this denial was unprecedented but it was upheld by another judge in October.
Abu Marzook had appealed the rulings and a U.S. government response to his appeal had been due on Wednesday.

During the news conference, lawyers played a taped statement from Abu Marzook in which he maintained his innocence and said his continued imprisonment only served the political interests of the Israeli government.

"Regrettably it seems that the U.S. has set aside all of its standards of justice in order to join with Israel in the political purpose of putting me in jail for no other reason than my leadership position in the political bureau of Hamas," Abu Marzook said.

He noted that he had been denied a hearing to raise the political offence exception to the extradition treaty. "This has never happened before. But it is clear that a Palestinian and Moslem cannot expect the same American quality of justice as others when Israeli interests are involved," he said.

Abu Marzook said that instead of continuing to be a part of an unfair process he was ready to go to Israel where he will get a hearing on the "absurd" charges. "Ultimately I may stand a better chance before Israeli judges than before New York judges."

M. Cherif Bassiouni, a Chicago lawyer who also represents Abu Marzook, said there was concern that his client will be tortured and possibly even killed in Israel. "Israel does use force in interrogation. We're quite fearful for him," he said.

Asked about reports that Hamas has threatened new suicide attacks in Israel if Abu Marzook stands trial there, Bassiouni said his client has condemned violence and would not encourage attacks. He characterised Abu Marzook as a "Gandhi-type leader" who would accept the "martyrdom he anticipates."
